label: Geometry, Algebra, Algorithms
notes: Open the course, spanning printed pages 1 through 48. The central theme is the dictionary between geometry and algebra: systems of polynomial equations define geometric objects called varieties, while the polynomials themselves generate algebraic objects called ideals. Algorithms make this correspondence computable, and this opening chapter introduces all three threads at once.

label: Polynomials and Affine Space
notes: We work over a field and consider polynomials in several variables, whose coefficients live in that field. Affine space is the set of all coordinate tuples over the field. A polynomial determines a function on affine space, and our objects of study are the common solution sets of collections of such polynomials.

label: Affine Varieties
notes: An affine variety is the set of points in affine space where a given collection of polynomials all vanish simultaneously. Lines, planes, circles, and twisted cubics are all examples. Unions and intersections of varieties are again varieties, giving the geometry a rich structure mirrored by algebraic operations on the defining equations.

label: Ideals
notes: The set of all polynomial combinations of a fixed collection forms an ideal, the algebraic shadow of a variety. Every polynomial in the ideal vanishes on the variety. Studying the ideal generated by the defining equations, rather than the equations themselves, gives a robust algebraic handle independent of how the equations were written.

label: Division in One Variable
notes: In one variable the division algorithm expresses any polynomial as a multiple of a divisor plus a remainder of lower degree. This makes the polynomial ring in one variable a principal ideal domain, where every ideal is generated by a single greatest common divisor, computed efficiently by the Euclidean algorithm.

label: Algorithmic Questions
notes: The chapter frames the driving computational problems: deciding whether a polynomial lies in an ideal, whether two varieties are equal, and how to describe a variety explicitly. Single-variable division solves the easy cases, but the multivariable versions demand the Grobner basis machinery developed next. Next: Grobner bases.
